title: A Blessed Birth
subtitle: The Coming of Muhammad ﷺ and the Household of Aminah
summary: The noble ancestry of the Prophet, the marriage of 'Abdullah and Aminah, the untimely loss of his father in Yathrib, the joyful birth in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant, and the naming of Muhammad by 'Abd al-Muttalib.

sections.text: The Lineage of Nobility and Moral Distinction

Throughout the turbulent centuries of pre-Islamic Arabia, lineage remained the cornerstone of social prestige, moral obligation, and communal memory. Within this genealogical framework, the ancestry of Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ﷺ stood at the pinnacle of honor. Traced meticulously by classical genealogists through Hashim, 'Abd Manaf, Qusayy, and Fihr to 'Adnan, his lineage connected directly to Prophet Isma'il and his father Ibrahim, peace be upon them.

The clan of Banu Hashim was distinguished not by vast mercantile monopolies or aggressive military posturing, but by moral dignity, civic generosity, and an unblemished reputation for integrity. Its leaders were guardians of the sacred well of Zamzam and providers of hospitality to pilgrims journeying from the farthest corners of the Arabian peninsula.
The ancient stone dwellings of Makkah nestled against the steep granite slopes of the Hijaz.
The Union of 'Abdullah and Aminah

Among the ten sons of 'Abd al-Muttalib, none was more cherished than his youngest, 'Abdullah. Renowned for his handsome countenance, upright conduct, and modesty, 'Abdullah had narrowly escaped sacrificial dedication in his youth when his father fulfilled a solemn vow by ransoming him with one hundred prime camels—an episode celebrated across Makkah.

When 'Abdullah attained manhood, 'Abd al-Muttalib sought for him a bride of equal nobility and refined character. His choice fell upon Aminah bint Wahb, daughter of the chieftain of the Banu Zuhrah clan of Quraysh. Recognized as the foremost maiden of her tribe in lineage, virtue, and grace, Aminah was wed to 'Abdullah in a ceremony attended by the elders of both families, establishing a household grounded in mutual respect and reverence.
The Shadow of Loss: 'Abdullah's Journey to Yathrib

According to reports collected by Ibn Sa'd, only a few months after the marriage 'Abdullah set out with a Qurayshi trading caravan toward Gaza and southern Syria, leaving his young bride expecting their first child.

On the return journey 'Abdullah fell ill. When the caravan reached the oasis of Yathrib (later known as Madinah), he was unable to continue to Makkah and stayed behind with his father's maternal kinsmen of Banu 'Adiyy ibn al-Najjar.
The long, solitary caravan trail winding through the arid mountains toward northern oases.

When the caravan arrived in Makkah without him, 'Abd al-Muttalib sent his eldest son, al-Harith, to Yathrib to bring his brother home. Al-Harith found that 'Abdullah had already died and been buried in the house of al-Nabighah. This is the account Ibn Sa'd transmits from al-Waqidi, which gives his age as twenty-five; other ages are also reported. Ibn Ishaq likewise places his death while Aminah was still pregnant, but some reports say he died a few months after the birth.
On the view of most biographers, then, the Prophet ﷺ was born an orphan. The Qur'an later recalls this to him: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?' (Surah Ad-Duha 93:6).
A Serene Pregnancy and Prophetic Portents

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Sa'd transmit reports that Aminah said she felt none of the usual heaviness of pregnancy. She is also reported to have said that she saw a light come forth from her by which the palaces of Busra in Syria were lit up. Later writers saw in this report a sign of the guidance her son would bring; such reports are found in the sirah literature and vary in the strength of their chains.
The Dawn of Rabi' al-Awwal

The birth took place in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant, corresponding approximately to 570 or 571 CE. An authentic hadith in Sahih Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ said he was born on a Monday. The month is generally given as Rabi' al-Awwal, though the exact day is disputed among historians; the 2nd, 8th, 9th and 12th are among the dates proposed.

Some later reports, whose chains are weak, name al-Shifa bint 'Awf (the mother of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf) among the women who attended the birth. Barakah, known as Umm Ayman, the Abyssinian woman who had belonged to 'Abdullah's household, cared for the child and remained devoted to him throughout his life.
Dawn light breaking softly over the craggy peaks surrounding the sanctuary of Makkah.
Thanksgiving in the Sacred House

Ibn Ishaq relates that after the birth Aminah sent word to 'Abd al-Muttalib: 'A boy has been born to you; come and look at him.' The grandfather came, looked at the child, and Aminah told him what she had seen during her pregnancy.

Ibn Ishaq continues that 'Abd al-Muttalib took the infant and went with him into the Ka'bah, where he stood praying to God and thanking Him for what He had given him, before returning the child to his mother.
The Name: Muhammad

A report found in later sirah works relates that on the seventh day 'Abd al-Muttalib held a feast for Quraysh, and that when they had eaten they asked him what he had named the child. He answered: 'I have named him Muhammad.'

'Why have you turned away from the names of your forefathers?' they asked, for the name was rare among the Arabs. He replied: 'I wished that God would praise him in heaven and His creation would praise him on earth.' — A report in later sirah works; its chain is regarded as weak

Derived from the Arabic root h-m-d (denoting continuous, abundant praise), the name Muhammad signifies 'The One Who is Praised Again and Again.' In his earliest infancy, the child was nursed by his loving mother Aminah for several days, followed by Thuwaybah, the maidservant of his paternal uncle Abu Lahab. Thuwaybah had recently suckled her own son Masruh as well as the Prophet's uncle Hamzah, establishing an early bond of foster brotherhood between them. Thus began, in tranquil humility, the earthly life of an orphan whose character would transform the moral conscience of the world.
